transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-18
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Ruth Zhang (Redwood SE), Evan Li (Redwood SRE); Marcus Hayes, Priya Singh, Daniel Cho, Jamal Ortiz (Tau Sector)

Summary (auto):
Technical deep dive focused on KV cache eviction/paging when supporting long-context conversational prompts and heavy prefix reuse. Reviewed Tau's workload patterns, memory limits, observed eviction symptoms, and proposed config and operational experiments (paging thresholds, prefix pinning, eviction policy tuning, and per-shard sizing). Agreed next steps to run staged benchmarks and share runbook + sizing spreadsheet.

Topics: KV cache architecture, eviction triggers, paging behavior, prefix reuse, batching impacts, quantization interactions, VPC/on-prem constraints for private deployments.

Shared artifacts referenced:
- Runbook: https://redwood.share/kv-eviction-runbook.pdf (referenced)
- Benchmarks: shared/benchmarks/tau-kv-runs.csv
- Config example gist: https://gist.github.com/redwood/kv-config-examples

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: All right thanks everyone for joining. we're going to do a deep dive on your KV cache eviction and paging issues. quick round robin — can you confirm who we have?
[00:08] Marcus: yeah Marcus here, CTO. Priya, Daniel, Jamal are on.
[00:12] Priya: hi, thanks. we've been hitting regular context drops in production when sessions exceed ~120k tokens, and we suspect KV eviction is kicking in and paged pages aren't coming back in fast enough.
[00:23] Ruth: yeah hi I'm Ruth, I'm the SE on this. quick note — some transcriptions call our product red wood inference or red wood, so apologies if terms shift in notes.
[00:30] Daniel: quick question before we jump: are we assuming Azure NVME or AWS instances? we are on private VPC with bare-metal-ish shaped instances.
[00:38] Evan: from Redwood side we saw your infra notes — looks like you run on a GCP-like equivalent with local NVMe and 1TB GPU mem per node, with 2 shards per GPU. correct?
[00:48] Marcus: correct, two GPUs per machine, each GPU pins two shards.
[00:52] Samir: ok great. quick agenda, we'll review your request patterns, show what eviction looks like on our side, then propose experiments: pinning hot prefixes, adjusting eviction windows, enabling paging with page-in thresholds, and some batching recommendations.

[01:10] Priya: to be explicit — most users reuse the same few prefixes (user profile + instructions) across many sessions, so prefix reuse is high. but long user messages sometimes append long history that expands KV size.
[01:23] Ruth: that's classic prefix reuse + long-context interplay. the KV cache is per-shard, and eviction is triggered by total KV size exceeding configured per-shard limit. currently tau's per-shard kv limit seems low relative to your workload so frequent LRU-style evictions happen.
[01:41] Daniel: can you remind us what eviction policy you use? is it strict LRU or approximate LRU?
[01:46] Ruth: default is an LRU-approx with windowed sampling — it's not perfect LRU. we do periodic compaction and also have a paging mode where older KV entries are moved to NVMe pages. the problem is page-in latency when that prefix is suddenly needed again.
[02:02] Samir: exactly. eviction = immediate drop; paging = move to local NVMe with a page-in penalty. both can cause increased latency or token hallucinations if the KV isn't available when decoding.
[02:12] Marcus: our symptom is that after a 70s spike of traffic with many concurrent sessions, we see downstream generations get shorter or lose context mid-turn. logs show token mismatch and kv-miss events.
[02:23] Evan: are those kv-miss counters high across specific shards or uniform?
[02:26] Priya: mostly concentrated on shard 1 and 2 on machine A. seems correlated with batching spikes — when batch size grows beyond 16 concurrent requests.
[02:35] Ruth: batching can exacerbate memory pressure because more KV entries are materialized in GPU cache simultaneously. two levers: reduce concurrency or increase per-shard KV size, or enable paging with more aggressive prefetching.

[03:00] Daniel: what about prefix pinning? can we mark the common prefixes as 'never-evict'?
[03:05] Samir: yes, we support prefix pinning. it's a tradeoff: pinned prefixes are resident in GPU memory and reduce eviction for hot keys, but they consume memory and hurt overall paging behavior. For heavy prefix reuse it's usually worth it.
[03:19] Ruth: we recommend pinning the small set of instruction + user-profile tokens and only pin the compact representation, not the entire expanded history. also consider canonicalizing prefixes so minor differences don't create separate entries.
[03:33] Priya: canonicalizing — we do sometimes include ephemeral session IDs in system prompts; that's probably fragmenting keys. good catch.
[03:40] Marcus: ok we'll scrub session IDs out of the prefix.

[04:00] Samir: let's talk numbers. current per-shard kv limit we saw in your config is 18GB. at your observed distribution (p90 context length ~80k tokens) we estimate needing ~26-32GB per shard to avoid eviction. that's why paging/eviction is happening under peak concurrency.
[04:19] Evan: is that estimate accounting for quantized weights or memory saved by int8 kernels?
[04:24] Ruth: this is KV cache memory, not model weight memory. quantization affects weights and runtime footprint but KV entries are token-level key/value pairs that scale with sequence length and hidden size; quantization doesn't reduce KV memory.
[04:36] Daniel: ok that clarifies.

[05:00] Priya: you mentioned prefetching. how aggressive can we be without hurting latency?
[05:05] Ruth: we have a page-in prefetch policy tuned by two parameters: page_size (MB) and readahead_window (number of subsequent tokens). for your workload we recommend readahead_window of 128 tokens and page_size tuned to your NVMe bandwidth; start small (64MB) and iterate. too large prefetch floods PCIe and impacts throughput.
[05:25] Samir: also set page_in_threshold to 0.3 (fraction of cache misses) for aggressive prefetch. we'll include recommended baseband values in the runbook.

[06:00] Marcus: what about eviction cadence? can we delay evictions slightly to avoid churn during bursts?
[06:06] Ruth: yes there's an eviction_backoff config so evictions are suspended for short windows after sudden memory growth; that reduces churn but temporarily increases peak memory and could OOM if not sized properly. for bursts we suggest combining backoff + ephemeral burst capacity (autoscale) or throttling concurrency.
[06:26] Priya: autoscale isn't trivial for our private deployment in VPC. we prefer tuning to avoid autoscale.
[06:31] Evan: one practical experiment: increase per-shard limit to 28GB for a canary subset of traffic for 24 hours, enable prefix pinning for top 3 prefixes, and enable readahead 64MB/128 tokens. measure kv-miss and page-in tail latency.
[06:47] Samir: yep that's our suggested experiment and we'll provide the sizing spreadsheet to justify memory bump.

[07:10] Daniel: can quantization of activations help reduce KV size? we've seen suggestions about kv compression.
[07:16] Ruth: we have an experimental compressed-kv option that reduces KV memory by ~20-30% by using 8-bit packing for values, but it increases CPU work during page-in and slightly affects latency. It's not recommended for strict latency SLOs but helpful when memory is severely constrained.
[07:33] Samir: also watch out for model-specific behaviors — some decoder architectures have larger KV per token. we'll share per-model multipliers in the repo.

[08:00] Priya: about paging backend — is NVMe on local disk required for paging? or can we use network-attached storage?
[08:06] Ruth: local NVMe is strongly recommended; network-attached storage (NFS/EFS) has unpredictable latency which kills page-in. we have a tiered paging prototype that can use remote object storage but with much higher latencies — not suitable for sub-200ms SLOs.
[08:23] Marcus: ours is local NVMe so good.

[08:40] Evan: anything else on prefix reuse? we've noticed lots of near-duplicate prefixes because of templating differences.
[08:46] Samir: canonicalization is low-hanging fruit. strip metadata tokens and normalize whitespace and punctuation. also consider a small LRU cache for prefix fingerprints to avoid creating many small KV entries for near-duplicates.
[09:02] Priya: finger prints — are there privacy issues?
[09:05] Ruth: fingerprints are hashed and stored ephemeral — we don't store raw user PII in prefix keys. but your compliance team should sign off.

[09:30] Marcus: about observability — what markers should we collect from our side to help you diagnose?
[09:35] Ruth: collect kv_mem_usage_per_shard, kv_eviction_count, kv_page_in_latency_p50/p95/p99, batch_size_distribution, concurrent_sessions, and a sample of a few request payloads (anonymized). also include model version and sequence length histograms.
[09:56] Samir: we'll send a prescriptive grafana dashboard and the runbook with exact metric names.

[10:20] Jamal: any quick wins we can do now?
[10:23] Samir: yes — canonicalize prefixes to reduce fragmentation, pin the top 3 prefixes, and increase per-shard kv limit for a small canary group. those three often cut eviction events by half.
[10:35] Priya: we'll do canonicalization and pinning this week.

[11:00] Daniel: can you walk through a concrete example of an eviction -> paging -> page-in timeline? we saw in logs a 400ms spike when a page-in occurred.
[11:08] Ruth: sure. timeline: at t0 eviction moves older KV entries to NVMe. at t1 a request needs the evicted prefix; it triggers a page-in which reads NVMe -> decompress -> copy over PCIe -> GPU. depending on page size and NVMe bandwidth this can be 50-500ms. if page-in overlaps with batching you can see amplified tail latency.
[11:33] Evan: so smaller pages mean more IOPS but lower tail per-page latency?
[11:38] Ruth: correct. smaller page_size reduces per-page read time but increases random IO. tuning depends on NVMe throughput and IOPS.

[12:00] Samir: operational checklist we'll provide: metrics to collect, alert thresholds (kv_eviction_rate > X per min), canary config, and exact config flags (eviction_backoff_seconds, kv_shard_size_gb, page_size_mb, readahead_tokens).
[12:18] Marcus: will you share the exact flag names? our infra team wants to script toggles.
[12:22] Ruth: yes included in the runbook and example terraform snippet.

[12:40] Priya: one last concern: we run heavy quantized models (int8) — does that affect page-in CPU cost?
[12:47] Samir: quantized models change kernel paths for weights but KV page-in CPU mostly depends on decompression and memcpy. compressed-kv will add CPU for unpacking. we'll include CPU cost estimates for compressed vs uncompressed KV in the spreadsheet.

[13:10] Jamal: what's the recommended SLO impact to expect after these changes?
[13:14] Ruth: with pinning + increase to 28GB + 64MB readahead you should see kv-miss reduction of 60-80% and page-in tail latency drop, translating to 30-50% fewer context-loss incidents in your observed workload. numbers dependent on exact distribution though.

[13:40] Samir: recap and next steps: we'll send the sizing spreadsheet, runbook, and a small terraform snippet for toggling flags. Ruth will run the paging experiment on our staging harness and provide logs. Marcus will provide token distribution + sample prefixes. schedule follow-up for next Tuesday.
[13:58] Marcus: sounds good. thanks.
[14:05] Priya: thanks everyone.

[14:20] End meeting.

Notes: transcript contains occasional filler and minor transcription errors (product names, acronyms). Action items recorded above.
